entries.f8dc8e4d3a58206f59c7138c93d78d3dac58a6cc: <div sID="gen2570" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="Lev.22" sID="Lev.22"/> <div eID="gen2570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2571" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2572" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have divers laws concerning the priests and sacrifices all for the preserving of the honour of the sanctuary. I. That the priests should not eat the holy things in their uncleanness, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.1-Lev.22.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. That no stranger who did not belong to some family of the priests should eat of the holy things (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.10-Lev.22.13">ver. 10-13</reference>), and, if he did it unwittingly, he must make restitution,, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.14-Lev.22.16">ver. 14-16</reference>. III. That the sacrifices which were offered must be without blemish, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.17-Lev.22.25">ver. 17-25</reference>. IV. That they must be more than eight days old (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.26-Lev.22.28">ver. 26-28</reference>), and that the sacrifices of thanksgiving must be eaten the same day they were offered, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.29-Lev.22.33">ver. 29</reference>, &c.
entries.ab8807adeefcc96c667cede37d2b1403dec55ba9: <div eID="gen2572" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2571" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Laws Concerning the Priests. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2573" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Speak unto Aaron and to his sons, that they separate themselves from the holy things of the children of Israel, and that they profane not my holy name <hi type="italic">in those things</hi> which they hallow unto me: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">3</hi> Say unto them, Whosoever <hi type="italic">he be</hi> of all your seed among your generations, that goeth unto the holy things, which the children of Israel hallow unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , having his uncleanness upon him, that soul shall be cut off from my presence: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">4</hi> What man soever of the seed of Aaron <hi type="italic">is</hi> a leper, or hath a running issue; he shall not eat of the holy things, until he be clean. And whoso toucheth any thing <hi type="italic">that is</hi> unclean <hi type="italic">by</hi> the dead, or a man whose seed goeth from him; <hi type="super">5</hi> Or whosoever toucheth any creeping thing, whereby he may be made unclean, or a man of whom he may take uncleanness, whatsoever uncleanness he hath; <hi type="super">6</hi> The soul which hath touched any such shall be unclean until even, and shall not eat of the holy things, unless he wash his flesh with water. <hi type="super">7</hi> And when the sun is down, he shall be clean, and shall afterward eat of the holy things; because it <hi type="italic">is</hi> his food. <hi type="super">8</hi> That which dieth of itself, or is torn <hi type="italic">with beasts,</hi> he shall not eat to defile himself therewith: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> They shall therefore keep mine ordinance, lest they bear sin for it, and die therefore, if they profane it: I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> do sanctify them. <div eID="gen2573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2574" type="x-p"/> Those that had a natural blemish, though they were forbidden to do the priests' work, were yet allowed to eat of the holy things: and the Jewish writers say that "to keep them from idleness they were employed in the wood-room, to pick out that which was worm-eaten, that it might not be used in the fire upon the altar; they might also be employed in the judgment of leprosy:" but, <div eID="gen2574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2575" type="x-p"/> I. Those that were under any ceremonial uncleanness, which possibly they contracted by their own fault, might no so much as eat of the holy things while they continued in their pollution. 1. Some pollutions were permanent, as a leprosy or a running issue, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.4">v. 4</reference>. These separated the people from the sanctuary, and God would show that they were so far from being more excusable that really they were more abominable in a priest. 2. Others were more transient, as the touching of a dead body, or any thing else that was unclean, from which, after a certain time, a man was cleansed by bathing his flesh in water, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.6">v. 6</reference>. But whoever was thus defiled might not <hi type="italic">eat of the holy things,</hi> under pain of God's highest displeasure, who said, and ratified the saying, <hi type="italic">That soul shall be cut off from my presence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.22.3">v. 3</reference>. Our being in the presence of God, and attending upon him, will be so far from securing us that it will but the more expose us to God's wrath, if we dare to draw nigh to him in our uncleanness. The destruction shall come <hi type="italic">from the presence of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.9">2 Thess. i. 9</reference>), as the fire by which Nadab and Abihu died came <hi type="italic">from before the Lord.</hi> Thus those who profane the holy word of God will be cut off by that word which they make so light of; it shall condemn them. They are again warned of their danger if they eat the holy thing in their uncleanness (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">lest they bear sin, and die therefore.</hi> Note, (1.) Those contract great guilt who profane sacred things, by touching them with unhallowed hands. Eating the holy things signified an interest in the atonement; but, if they ate of them in their uncleanness, they were so far from lessening their guilt that they increased it: They shall <hi type="italic">bear sin.</hi> (2.) Sin is a burden which, if infinite mercy prevent not, will certainly sink those that bear it: They shall <hi type="italic">die therefore.</hi> Even priests may be ruined by their pollutions and presumptions. <div eID="gen2575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2576" type="x-p"/> II. As to the design of this law we may observe, 1. This obliged the priests carefully to preserve their purity, and to dread every thing that would defile them. The holy things were their livelihood; if they might not eat of them, how must they subsist? The more we have to lose of comfort and honour by our defilement, the more careful we should be to preserve our purity. 2. This impressed the people with a reverence for the holy things, when they saw the priests themselves <hi type="italic">separated from them</hi> (as the expression is, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.2">v. 2</reference>) so long as they were in their uncleanness. He is doubtless a God of infinite purity who kept his immediate attendants under so strict a discipline. 3. This teaches us carefully to watch against all moral pollutions, because by them we are unfitted to receive the comfort of God's sanctuary. Though we labour not under habitual deformities, yet actual defilements deprive us of the pleasure of communion with God; and therefore <hi type="italic">he that is washed needeth to wash his feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.13.10">John xiii. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">to wash his hands,</hi> and so to <hi type="italic">compass the altar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.26.6">Ps. xxvi. 6</reference>. Herein we have need to be jealous over ourselves, lest (as it is observably expressed here) we <hi type="italic">profane God's holy name in those things which we hallow unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.22.2">v. 2</reference>. If we affront God in those very performances wherein we pretend to honour him, and provoke him instead of pleasing him, we shall make up but a bad account shortly; yet thus we do if we profane God's name, by doing that in our uncleanness which pretends to be hallowed to him.
entries.f684236b9f876c1fbba9d9f35ef5077316f264d9: <div eID="gen2576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2577" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> There shall no stranger eat <hi type="italic">of</hi> the holy thing: a sojourner of the priest, or an hired servant, shall not eat <hi type="italic">of</hi> the holy thing. <hi type="super">11</hi> But if the priest buy <hi type="italic">any</hi> soul with his money, he shall eat of it, and he that is born in his house: they shall eat of his meat. <hi type="super">12</hi> If the priest's daughter also be <hi type="italic">married</hi> unto a stranger, she may not eat of an offering of the holy things. <hi type="super">13</hi> But if the priest's daughter be a widow, or divorced, and have no child, and is returned unto her father's house, as in her youth, she shall eat of her father's meat: but there shall no stranger eat thereof. 14 And if a man eat <hi type="italic">of</hi> the holy thing unwittingly, then he shall put the fifth <hi type="italic">part</hi> thereof unto it, and shall give <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto the priest with the holy thing. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they shall not profane the holy things of the children of Israel, which they offer unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; 16 Or suffer them to bear the iniquity of trespass, when they eat their holy things: for I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> do sanctify them. <div eID="gen2577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2578" type="x-p"/> The holy things were to be eaten by the priests and their families. Now, <div eID="gen2578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2579" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a law that no stranger should eat of them, that is, no person whatsoever but the priests only, and those that pertained to them, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.10">v. 10</reference>. The priests are charged with this care, not to <hi type="italic">profane the holy things</hi> by permitting the strangers to eat of them (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.15">v. 15</reference>) or <hi type="italic">suffer them to bear the iniquity of trespass</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.16">v. 16</reference>); that is, suffer them to bring guilt upon themselves, by meddling with that which they have no right to. Thus it is commonly understood. Note, We must not only be careful that we do not bear iniquity ourselves, but we must do what we can to prevent others bearing it. We must not only not suffer sin to <hi type="italic">lie</hi> upon our brother, but, if we can help it, we must not suffer it to <hi type="italic">come</hi> upon him. But perhaps there is another meaning of those words: the priests' eating the sin-offerings is said to signify their <hi type="italic">bearing the iniquity of the congregation, to make an atonement for them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.10.17">ch. x. 17</reference>. Let not a stranger therefore eat of that holy thing particularly, and so pretend to <hi type="italic">bear the iniquity of trespass;</hi> for it is daring presumption for any to do that, but such as are appointed to do it. Those that set up other mediators besides Christ our priest, to <hi type="italic">bear the iniquity of trespass,</hi> sacrilegiously rob Christ of his honour, and invade his rights. When we warn people not to trust to their own righteousness, nor dare to appear before God in it, but to rely on Christ's righteousness only for peace and pardon, it is because we dare not <hi type="italic">suffer them to bear the iniquity of trespass,</hi> for we know it is too heavy for them. <div eID="gen2579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2580" type="x-p"/> II. Here is an explanation of the law, showing who were to be looked upon as belonging to the priest's family, and who not. 1. Sojourners and hired servants abode not in the house for ever; they were in the family, but not of it; and therefore they might not eat of the holy things (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.10">v. 10</reference>): but the servant that was born in the house or bought with money, being a heirloom to the family, though a servant, yet might eat of the holy things, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, Those only are entitled to the comforts of God's house who make it their <hi type="italic">rest for ever,</hi> and resolve to <hi type="italic">dwell in it all the days of their life.</hi> As for those who for a time only believe, to serve a present turn. They are looked upon but as sojourners and mercenaries, and have <hi type="italic">no part nor lot in the matter.</hi> 2. As to the children of the family, concerning the sons there could be no dispute, they were themselves priests, but concerning the daughters there was a distinction. While they continued in their father's house they might eat of the holy things; but, if they married such as were not priests, they lost their right (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.12">v. 12</reference>), for now they were cut off from the family of the priests. Yet if a priest's daughter became a widow, and had no children in whom she might preserve a distinct family, and returned to her father's house again, being neither wife nor mother, she should again be looked upon as a daughter, and might eat of the holy things. If those whom Providence has made sorrowful widows, and who are dislodged from the rest they had in the house of a husband, yet find it again in a father's house, they have reason to be thankful to the widows' God, who does not leave them comfortless. 3. Here is a demand of restitution to be made by him that had no right to the holy things, and yet should eat of them unwittingly, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.14">v. 14</reference>. If he did it presumptuously, and in contempt of the divine institution, he was liable to be cut off by the hand of God, and to be beaten by the magistrate; but, if he did it through weakness in inconsideration, he was to restore the value, adding a fifth part to it, besides which he was to bring an offering to atone for the trespass; see <reference osisRef="Lev.5.15-Lev.5.16">ch. v. 15, 16</reference>. <div eID="gen2580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2581" type="x-p"/> III. This law might be dispensed with in a case of necessity, as it was when David and his men ate of the show-bread, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.6">1 Sam. xxi. 6</reference>. And our Saviour justifies them, and gives a reason for it, which furnishes us with a lasting rule in all such cases, that <hi type="italic">God will have mercy and not sacrifice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.12.3-Matt.12.4">Matt. xii. 3, 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.7">7</reference>. Rituals must give way to morals. <div eID="gen2581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2582" type="x-p"/> IV. It is an instruction to gospel ministers, who are <hi type="italic">stewards of the mysteries of God,</hi> not to admit all, without distinction, to <hi type="italic">eat of the holy things,</hi> but to take out the precious from the vile. Those that are scandalously ignorant or profane are strangers and aliens to the family of the Lord's priests; and it is not meet to take the children's bread and to cast it to such. Holy things are for holy persons, for those who are holy, at least, in profession, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Matt. vii. 6</reference>.
entries.6a45b8a95fd4422669773ebba19a6a13066bb018: <div eID="gen2582" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Laws Concerning Sacrifices. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2583" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">18</hi> Speak unto Aaron, and to his sons, and unto all the children of Israel, and say unto them, Whatsoever <hi type="italic">he be</hi> of the house of Israel, or of the strangers in Israel, that will offer his oblation for all his vows, and for all his freewill offerings, which they will offer unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for a burnt offering; <hi type="super">19</hi> <hi type="italic">Ye shall offer</hi> at your own will a male without blemish, of the beeves, of the sheep, or of the goats. <hi type="super">20</hi> <hi type="italic">But</hi> whatsoever hath a blemish, <hi type="italic">that</hi> shall ye not offer: for it shall not be acceptable for you. <hi type="super">21</hi> And whosoever offereth a sacrifice of peace offerings unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to accomplish <hi type="italic">his</hi> vow, or a freewill offering in beeves or sheep, it shall be perfect to be accepted; there shall be no blemish therein. <hi type="super">22</hi> Blind, or broken, or maimed, or having a wen, or scurvy, or scabbed, ye shall not offer these unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , nor make an offering by fire of them upon the altar unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">23</hi> Either a bullock or a lamb that hath any thing superfluous or lacking in his parts, that mayest thou offer <hi type="italic">for</hi> a freewill offering; but for a vow it shall not be accepted. <hi type="super">24</hi> Ye shall not offer unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that which is bruised, or crushed, or broken, or cut; neither shall ye make <hi type="italic">any offering thereof</hi> in your land. <hi type="super">25</hi> Neither from a stranger's hand shall ye offer the bread of your God of any of these; because their corruption <hi type="italic">is</hi> in them, <hi type="italic">and</hi> blemishes <hi type="italic">be</hi> in them: they shall not be accepted for you. <hi type="super">26</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">27</hi> When a bullock, or a sheep, or a goat, is brought forth, then it shall be seven days under the dam; and from the eighth day and thenceforth it shall be accepted for an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">28</hi> And <hi type="italic">whether it be</hi> cow or ewe, ye shall not kill it and her young both in one day. <hi type="super">29</hi> And when ye will offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , offer <hi type="italic">it</hi> at your own will. <hi type="super">30</hi> On the same day it shall be eaten up; ye shall leave none of it until the morrow: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">31</hi> Therefore shall ye keep my commandments, and do them: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">32</hi> Neither shall ye profane my holy name; but I will be hallowed among the children of Israel: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which hallow you, 33 That brought you out of the land of Egypt, to be your God: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen2583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2584" type="x-p"/> Here are four laws concerning sacrifices:— <div eID="gen2584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2585" type="x-p"/> I. Whatever was offered in sacrifice to God should be without blemish, otherwise it should not be accepted. This had often been mentioned in the particular institutions of the several sorts of offerings. Now here they are told what was to be accounted a blemish which rendered a beast unfit for sacrifice: if it was blind, or lame, had a wen, or the mange (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.22">v. 22</reference>),—if it was bruised, or crushed, or broken, or cut (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.24">v. 24</reference>), that is, as the Jewish writers understand it, if it was, in any of these ways, castrated, if bulls and rams were made into oxen and weathers, they might not be offered. Moreover a difference is made between what was brought as a free-will offering and what was brought as a vow, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.23">v. 23</reference>. And, though none that had any of the forementioned blemishes might be brought for either, yet if a beast had any thing superfluous or lacking (that is, as the Jews understand it, if there was a disproportion or inequality between those parts that are pairs, when one eye, or ear, or leg, was bigger than it should be, or less than it should be)—if there was no other blemish than this, it might be accepted for a free-will offering, to which a man had not before laid himself, nor had the divine law laid him, under any particular obligation; but for a vow it might not be accepted. Thus God would teach us to make conscience of performing our promises to him very exactly, and not afterwards to abate in quantity or value of what we had solemnly engaged to devote to him. What was, before the vow, in our own power, as in the case of a free-will offering, afterwards is not, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.4">Acts v. 4</reference>. It is again and again declared that no sacrifice should be accepted if it was thus blemished, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.20-Lev.22.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. According to this law great care was taken to search all the beasts that were brought to be sacrificed, that there might, to a certainty, be no blemish in them. A blemished sacrifice might not be accepted even <hi type="italic">from the hand of a stranger,</hi> though to such all possible encouragement should be given to do honour to the God of Israel, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.25">v. 25</reference>. By this it appears that strangers were expected to come to the house of God from a <hi type="italic">far country</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.41-1Kgs.8.42">1 Kings viii. 41, 42</reference>), and that they should be welcome, and their offerings accepted, as those of Darius, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.9-Ezra.6.10">Ezra vi. 9, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.56.6-Isa.56.7">Isa. lvi. 6, 7</reference>. The heathen priests were many of them not so strict in this matter, but would receive sacrifices for their gods that were ever so scandalous; but let strangers know that the God of Israel would not be so served. Now, 1. This law was then necessary for the preserving of the honour of the sanctuary, and of the God that was there worshipped. It was fit that every thing that was employed for his honour should be the best of the kind; for, as he is the greatest and brightest, so he is the best of beings; and he that is the best must have the best. See how greatly and justly displeasing the breach of this law was to the holy God, <reference osisRef="Mal.1.8">Mal. i. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mal.1.13">13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mal.1.14">14</reference>. 2. This law made all the legal sacrifices the fitter to be types of Christ, the great sacrifice from which all these derived their virtue. In allusion to this law, he is said to be <hi type="italic">a Lamb without blemish</hi> and <hi type="italic">without spot,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.19">1 Pet. i. 19</reference>. As such a priest, so such a sacrifice, became us, who was harmless and undefiled. When Pilate declared, <hi type="italic">I find no fault in this man,</hi> he did thereby in effect pronounce the sacrifice without blemish. The Jews say it was the work of the sagan, or suffragan, high priest, to view the sacrifices, and see whether they were without blemish or no; when Christ suffered, Annas was in that office; but little did those who brought Christ to Annas first, by whom he was sent bound to Caiaphas, as a sacrifice fit to be offered (<reference osisRef="John.18.13">John xviii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.18.24">24</reference>), think that they were answering the type of this law. 3. It is an instruction to us to offer to God the best we have in our spiritual sacrifices. If our devotions are ignorant, and cold, and trifling, and full of distractions, we offer <hi type="italic">the blind, and the lame, and the sick, for sacrifice;</hi> but cursed be the deceiver that does so, for, while he thinks to put a cheat upon God, he puts a damning cheat upon his own soul. <div eID="gen2585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2586" type="x-p"/> II. That no beast should be offered in sacrifice before it was eight days old, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.26-Lev.22.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. It was provided before that the firstlings of their cattle, which were to be dedicated to God, should not be brought to him till after the eighth day, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.30">Exod. xxii. 30</reference>. Here it is provided that no creature should be offered in sacrifice till it was eight days old complete. Sooner than that it was not fit to be used at men's tables, and therefore not a God's altar. The Jews say, "It was because the sabbath sanctifies all things, and nothing should be offered to God till at least one sabbath had passed over it." It was in conformity to the law of circumcision, which children were to receive on the eighth day. Christ was sacrificed for us, not in his infancy, though then Herod sought to slay him, but in the prime of his time. <div eID="gen2586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2587" type="x-p"/> III. That the dam and her young should not both be killed in one day, whether in sacrifice or for common use, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.28">v. 28</reference>. There is such a law as this concerning birds, <reference osisRef="Deut.22.6">Deut. xxii. 6</reference>. This was forbidden, not as evil in itself, but because it looked barbarous and cruel to the brute creatures; like the tyranny of the king of Babylon, that slew Zedekiah's sons before his eyes, and then put out his eyes. It looked ill-natured towards the species to kill two generations at once, as if one designed the ruin of the kind. <div eID="gen2587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2588" type="x-p"/> IV. That the flesh of their thank-offerings should be eaten on the same day that they were sacrificed, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.29-Lev.22.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. This is a repetition of what we had before, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.15">ch. vii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.6-Lev.19.7">xix. 6, 7</reference>. The chapter concludes with such a general charge as we have often met with, to <hi type="italic">keep God's commandments,</hi> and not to <hi type="italic">profane his holy name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.22.31-Lev.22.32">v. 31, 32</reference>. Those that profess God's name, if they do not make conscience of keeping his commandments, do but profane his name. The general reasons are added: God's authority over them—<hi type="italic">I am the Lord;</hi> his interest in them—I am <hi type="italic">your God;</hi> the title he had to them by redemption—"I <hi type="italic">brought you out of the land of Egypt,</hi> on purpose that I might be your God;" the designs of his grace concerning them—<hi type="italic">I am the Lord that hallow you;</hi> and the resolutions of his justice, if he had not honour from them, to <hi type="italic">get himself honour</hi> upon them—I will be <hi type="italic">hallowed among the children of Israel.</hi> God will be a loser in his glory by no man at last; but sooner or later will recover his right, either in the repentance of sinners or in their ruin.  <chapter eID="Lev.22"/> <div eID="gen2588" type="x-p"/>

entries.fa5a1584de4345cd84c7636e451cbba45cf73db9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1158"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 22</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.22.1-Lev.22.9">Le 22:1-9</reference>. The Priests in Their Uncleanness.</title> <div sID="gen1587" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1158"/><hi type="bold">2. Speak unto Aaron and to his sons, that they separate themselves from the holy things--</hi>"To separate" means, in the language of the Mosaic ritual, "to abstain"; and therefore the import of this injunction is that the priests should abstain from eating that part of the sacrifices which, though belonging to their order, was to be partaken of only by such of them as were free from legal impurities.<div eID="gen1587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1588" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they profane not my holy name in those things which they hallow unto me, &c.--</hi>that is, let them not, by their want of due reverence, give occasion to profane my holy name. A careless or irreverent use of things consecrated to God tends to dishonor the name and bring disrespect on the worship of God. <div eID="gen1588" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ed9d6a0a51b761e1fe08e8da3db3c5b57ddfcc6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1159"/><div sID="gen1589" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1159"/><hi type="bold">3. Whosoever he be ... that goeth unto the holy things--</hi>The multitude of minute restrictions to which the priests, from accidental defilement, were subjected, by keeping them constantly on their guard lest they should be unfit for the sacred service, tended to preserve in full exercise the feeling of awe and submission to the authority of God. The ideas of sin and duty were awakened in their breasts by every case to which either an interdict or an injunction was applied. But why enact an express statute for priests disqualified by the leprosy or polluting touch of a carcass [Le 22:4], when a general law was already in force which excluded from society all persons in that condition? Because priests might be apt, from familiarity, to trifle with religion, and in committing irregularities or sins, to shelter themselves under the cloak of the sacred office. This law, therefore, was passed, specifying the chief forms of temporary defilement which excluded from the sanctuary, that priests might not deem themselves entitled to greater license than the rest of the people; and that so far from being in any degree exempted from the sanctions of the law, they were under greater obligations, by their priestly station, to observe it in its strict letter and its smallest enactments. <div eID="gen1589" type="x-p"/>
entries.f157518af4792b7aa3240c0e6cf83729ad3040d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1160"/><div sID="gen1590" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1160"/><hi type="bold">4-6. wash his flesh with water--</hi>Any Israelite who had contracted a defilement of such a nature as debarred him from the enjoyment of his wonted privileges, and had been legally cleansed from the disqualifying impurity, was bound to indicate his state of recovery by the immersion of his whole person in water. Although all ceremonial impurity formed a ground of exclusion, there were degrees of impurity which entailed a longer or shorter period of excommunication, and for the removal of which different rites required to be observed according to the trivial or the malignant nature of the case. A person who came inadvertently into contact with an unclean animal was rendered unclean for a specified period; and then, at the expiry of that term, he washed, in token of his recovered purity. But a leper was unclean so long as he remained subject to that disease, and on his convalescence, he also washed, not to cleanse himself, for the water was ineffectual for that purpose, but to signify that he was clean. Not a single case is recorded of a leper being restored to communion by the use of water; it served only as an outward and visible sign that such a restoration was to be made. The Book of Leviticus abounds with examples which show that in all the ceremonial washings, as uncleanness meant loss of privileges, so baptism with water indicated a restoration to those privileges. There was no exemption; for as the unclean Israelite was exiled from the congregation, so the unclean priest was disqualified from executing his sacred functions in the sanctuary; and in the case of both, the same observance was required--a formal intimation of their being readmitted to forfeited privileges was intimated by the appointed rite of baptism. If any one neglected or refused to perform the washing, he disobeyed a positive precept, and he remained in his uncleanness; he forbore to avail himself of this privilege, and was therefore said to be "cut off" from the presence of the Lord. <div eID="gen1590" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fb2b3164d7d252a6ec03899bd35a82b477e2df1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1161"/><div sID="gen1591" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1161"/><hi type="bold">8. dieth of itself--</hi>The feelings of nature revolt against such food. It might have been left to the discretion of the Hebrews, who it may be supposed (like the people of all civilized nations) would have abstained from the use of it without any positive interdict. But an express precept was necessary to show them that whatever died naturally or from disease, was prohibited to them by the operation of that law which forbade them the use of any meat with its blood. <div eID="gen1591" type="x-p"/>
entries.e72824014456f3f594d69e241cd70a2e98b850ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1162"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.22.10-Lev.22.16">Le 22:10-16</reference>. Who of the Priests' House May Eat of Them.</title> <div sID="gen1592" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1162"/><hi type="bold">10-13. There shall no stranger eat the holy thing--</hi>The portion of the sacrifices assigned for the support of the officiating priests was restricted to the exclusive use of his own family. A temporary guest or a hired servant was not at liberty to eat of them; but an exception was made in favor of a bought or homeborn slave, because such was a stated member of his household. On the same principle, his own daughter, who married a husband not a priest, could not eat of them. However, if a widow and childless, she was reinstated in the privileges of her father's house as before her marriage. But if she had become a mother, as her children had no right to the privileges of the priesthood, she was under a necessity of finding support for them elsewhere than under her father's roof. <div eID="gen1592" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9c4d8bb06af996f63cfbf1c8d15805cd4dab458: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1164"/><div sID="gen1594" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1164"/><hi type="bold">14. if a man eat of the holy thing unwittingly--</hi>A common Israelite might unconsciously partake of what had been offered as tithes, first-fruits, &c., and on discovering his unintentional error, he was not only to restore as much as he had used, but be fined in a fifth part more for the priests to carry into the sanctuary. <div eID="gen1594" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb591376d7419411781b16aba4d915c2d45cf622: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1165"/><div sID="gen1595" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1165"/><hi type="bold">15-16. they shall not profane the holy things of the children of Israel--</hi>There is some difficulty felt in determining to whom "they" refers. The subject of the preceding context being occupied about the priests, it is supposed by some that this relates to them also; and the meaning then is that the whole people would incur guilt through the fault of the priests, if they should defile the sacred offerings, which they would have done had they presented them while under any defilement [Calvin]. According to others, "the children of Israel" is the nominative in the sentence; which thus signifies, the children of Israel shall not profane or defile their offerings, by touching them or reserving any part of them, lest they incur the guilt of eating what is divinely appointed to the priests alone [Calmet]. <div eID="gen1595" type="x-p"/>
entries.6510183fda29ec3e7172c94550d24c707a65e89f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1166"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.22.17-Lev.22.33">Le 22:17-33</reference>. The Sacrifices Must Be without Blemish.</title> <div sID="gen1596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1166"/><hi type="bold">19. Ye shall offer at your own will--</hi>rather, to your being accepted.<div eID="gen1596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1597" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a male without blemish--</hi>This law (<reference osisRef="Lev.1.3">Le 1:3</reference>) is founded on a sense of natural propriety, which required the greatest care to be taken in the selection of animals for sacrifice. The reason for this extreme caution is found in the fact that sacrifices are either an expression of praise to God for His goodness, or else they are the designed means of conciliating or retaining His favor. No victim that was not perfect in its kind could be deemed a fitting instrument for such purposes if we assume that the significance of sacrifices is derived entirely from their relation to Jehovah. Sacrifices may be likened to gifts made to a king by his subjects, and hence the reasonableness of God's strong remonstrance with the worldly-minded Jews (Mal 1:8). If the tabernacle, and subsequently the temple, were considered the palace of the great King, then the sacrifices would answer to presents as offered to a monarch on various occasions by his subjects; and in this light they would be the appropriate expressions of their feelings towards their sovereign. When a subject wished to do honor to his sovereign, to acknowledge allegiance, to appease his anger, to supplicate forgiveness, or to intercede for another, he brought a present; and all the ideas involved in sacrifices correspond to these sentiments--those of gratitude, of worship, of prayer, of confession and atonement [Bib. Sac.]. <div eID="gen1597" type="x-p"/>
entries.b642b6d8c7b59c0cabf403fbd9d3eaa5a74736bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1167"/><div sID="gen1598" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1167"/><hi type="bold">23. that mayest thou offer, &c.--</hi>The passage should be rendered thus: "if thou offer it either for a freewill offering, or for a vow, it shall not be accepted." This sacrifice being required to be "without blemish" [Le 22:19], symbolically implied that the people of God were to dedicate themselves wholly with sincere purposes of heart, and its being required to be "perfect to be accepted" [Le 22:21], led them typically to Him without whom no sacrifice could be offered acceptable to God. <div eID="gen1598" type="x-p"/>
entries.010dcc4fc0a0e6fc2e10088ed7745446c63c7ffc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1168"/><div sID="gen1599" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1168"/><hi type="bold">27-28. it shall be seven days under the dam--</hi>Animals were not considered perfect nor good for food till the eighth day. As sacrifices are called the bread or food of God (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.25">Le 22:25</reference>), to offer them immediately after birth, when they were unfit to be eaten, would have indicated a contempt of religion; and besides, this prohibition, as well as that contained in <reference osisRef="Lev.22.28">Le 22:28</reference>, inculcated a lesson of humanity or tenderness to the dam, as well as secured the sacrifices from all appearance of unfeeling cruelty. <chapter eID="Lev.22"/>

entries.0e678c102ce518f450c06209a6f7297d69a3b254: <div eID="gen4948" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4949" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4950" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4950" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4949" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4951" type="x-p"/> Of the uncleanness of the priests, by which they were prevented from ministering in holy things, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.1-Lev.22.5">Lev 22:1-5</reference>. How they should be cleansed, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.6">Lev 22:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.7">Lev 22:7</reference>. The priest must not eat of any animal that had died of itself, or was torn by wild beasts, but must keep God's ordinances, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.8">Lev 22:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.9">Lev 22:9</reference>. No stranger, sojourner, nor hired servant shall eat of the holy things, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.10">Lev 22:10</reference>. A servant bought with money may eat of them, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.11">Lev 22:11</reference>. Who of the priest's family may not eat of them, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.12">Lev 22:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.13">Lev 22:13</reference>. Of improper persons who partake of the holy things unknowingly, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.14-Lev.22.16">Lev 22:14-16</reference>. Freewill-offerings, and sacrifices in general, must be without blemish, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.17-Lev.22.25">Lev 22:17-25</reference>. The age at which different animals were to be offered to God, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.26">Lev 22:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.27">Lev 22:27</reference>. No animal and its young shall be offered on the same day, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.28">Lev 22:28</reference>. How the sacrifice of thanks-giving was to be offered, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.29">Lev 22:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.30">Lev 22:30</reference>. All God's testimonies to be observed, and the reason, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.31-Lev.22.33">Lev 22:31-33</reference>.
entries.486819d41e15d58151a922d0dd4e33889c31f4f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen4951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4952" type="x-p"/> Speak unto Aaron and to his sons, that they separate themselves - The same subject is continued in this chapter as in the preceding, with this addition, that besides the perfection of the priests, it was indispensably necessary that the sacrifices also should be perfect. In the service of God, according to the law, neither an imperfect offering nor an imperfect offerer could be admitted. What need then of a mediator between a holy God and sinful men! And can we expect that any of our services, however sincere and well-intentioned, can be accepted, unless offered on that living Altar that sanctifies the gift?
entries.41e7c1664e5d05d95418d96f9ae1eeaa3dbb578e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen4952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4953" type="x-p"/> Is a leper, or hath a running issue - See the case of the leper treated at large in the notes on Leviticus 13 (note) and Leviticus 14 (note); and for other uncleannesses, see the notes on Leviticus 15 (note).
entries.d39a4ebaf937169ded9f31e9e748c8fd13743a62: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen4953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4954" type="x-p"/> There shall no stranger eat of the holy thing - For the meaning of the word stranger, see the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.12.43">Exo 12:43</reference>. The Jews suppose that stranger here means one who has had his ear pierced, (see the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.21.6">Exo 21:6</reference>), and that sojourner means a servant who is to go free on the Sabbatical year. Neither of these was permitted to eat of the holy things, because they were not properly members of the priest's family, and might go out and defile themselves even with the abominations of the heathen; but the servant or slave that was bought with money, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.11">Lev 22:11</reference>, might eat of these things, because he was the property of the master for ever. We see that it was lawful, under the Mosaic economy, to have slaves under certain restrictions; but these were taken from among the heathen, and instructed in the true religion: hence we find, as in the above case, that they were reckoned as a part of the priest's own family, and treated as such. They certainly had privileges which did not extend either to sojourners or to hired servants; therefore their situation was incomparably better than the situation of the slaves under different European governments, of whose souls their pitiless possessors in general take no care, while they themselves venture to profess the Christian religion, and quote the Mosaic law in vindication of their system of slavery. How preposterous is such conduct! and how intolerable!
entries.26c1167ea402e4f5551567c6d6a365b6a4e763e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen4954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4955" type="x-p"/> But if the priest's daughter be a widow - and is returned unto her father's house - A widow in Bengal not infrequently returns to her father's house on the death of her husband: the union betwixt her and her own family is never so dissolved as among European nations. Thousands of widows in Bengal, whose husbands die before the consummation of marriage, never leave their parents - Ward.
entries.4df4f56b75b8d66f044140e574d34d7d96488660: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen4955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4956" type="x-p"/> Then he shall put the fifth part thereof unto it - The holy thing of which he has unknowingly eaten shall be fairly valued, and to this value he shall add one fifth more, and give the whole to the priest.
entries.78b32362036c48ccf17cab388fd8072be18bd065: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen4956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4957" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever hath a blemish - The same perfection is required in the sacrifice that was required in the priest; see on <reference osisRef="Lev.22.2">Lev 22:2</reference> (note), and the notes on Leviticus 21 (note).
entries.952f76d874a6afb2418cebd6088dd496062c0adc: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen4957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4958" type="x-p"/> That hath anything superfluous or lacking - The term שרוע sarua signifies any thing extended beyond the usual size, and the term קלוט kalut signifies any thing unusually contracted; and both mean any monstrosity, whether in redundance or defect. Such things, it seems, might be offered for a freewill-offering, because that was not prescribed by the law; God left it to a man's piety and gratitude to offer such additional gifts as he could: what the law required was indispensably necessary, because it pointed out the Gospel economy; but he that made a vow to offer such a sacrifice as the law had not required, could of course bring an imperfect offering. Some contend that the last clause of this verse should be thus read: If thou offer it either for a freewill-offering, or for a vow, it shall not be accepted. It was the opinion of the Jews, and it appears to be correct, that none of these imperfect animals were ever offered on the altar; but the person who made the freewill-offering of such things as he had, sold the animal, and gave its price for the support of the sanctuary.
entries.63b3c9df36a94c13d89c971228a8f5c702fb2c3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen4958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4959" type="x-p"/> Bruised, or crushed, or broken, or cut - That is, no bullock or lamb that is injured in any of the above ways, shall be offered unto the Lord.
entries.db816bb1256bba0d6b52beb7a40e9c91b112cc7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen4959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4960" type="x-p"/> Their corruption is in them - Viz., they are bruised, crushed, broken, etc.
entries.8fe5c1b999e38d341af1c771fc6668360e32775f: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen4960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4961" type="x-p"/> When a bullock - is brought forth - This is a most unfortunate as well as absurd translation. The creature called an ox is a bull castrated; surely then a bullock was never yet brought forth! The original word שור shor signifies a bull, a bullock, or indeed any thing of the neat kind: here, even common sense required that it should be translated calf; and did I not hold myself sacredly bound to print the text of the common version with scrupulous exactness, I should translate the former clause of this verse thus, and so enter it into the text: When a Calf, or a Lamb, or a Kid is brought forth, instead of, When a bullock, a sheep, or a goat is brought forth, the absurdity of which is glaring. <div eID="gen4961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4962" type="x-p"/> Seven days under the dam - In vindication of the propriety of this precept it may be justly asserted, that the flesh of very young animals is comparatively innutritive, and that animal food is not sufficiently nourishing and wholesome till the animal has arrived at a certain growth, or acquired the perfection of its nature. There is something brutish in eating the young of beast or fowl before the hair and hoofs are perfect in the one, and the feathers and claws in the other. Before this period their flesh is not good for food. See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.9.1">Lev 9:1</reference>.
entries.8b636ea40a6d7897c68f79f3360cb98555728af0: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen4962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4963" type="x-p"/> Ye shall not kill it and her young in one day - This precept was certainly intended to inculcate mercy and tenderness of heart; and so the Jews understood it. When it is necessary to take away the lives of innocent animals for the support of our own, we should do it in such a way as not to blunt our moral feelings; and deplore the necessity, while we feel an express gratitude to God for permission, to do it.
entries.a152a736175b43d6ddc3c32e440d771ba1d45726: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen4963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4964" type="x-p"/> Leave none of it until the morrow - See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.7.15">Lev 7:15</reference>.
entries.fa5b99906fea67738e8454fbebf409a14e94a5d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen4964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4965" type="x-p"/> Neither shall ye profane my holy name - God's name is profaned or rendered common when we treat his commands as we often do those of our fellows, when they do not appear to have self-interest to recommend them. He therefore profanes God's holy name who does not both implicitly believe and conscientiously obey all his words and all his precepts. <div eID="gen4965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4966" type="x-p"/> I will be hallowed among the children of Israel - The words children of Israel, בני ישראל beney Yishrael, which so frequently occur, should be translated either the descendants or posterity of Israel, or the people of Israel. The word children has a tendency to beget a false notion, especially in the minds of young people, and lead them to think that children, in the proper sense of the word, i. e., little ones, are meant.
entries.ddffe8d9392bc099dc96180464bcdbd19f879188: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen4966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4967" type="x-p"/> Brought you out of the land of Egypt - By such a series of miraculous interferences, to be your God - to save you from all idolatry, false and superstitious worship, teach you the right way, lead and support you in it, and preserve you to my eternal kingdom and glory. God, infinite in his own perfections, has no need of his creatures; but they need him; and, as a source of endless felicity, he opens himself to all his intelligent offspring.  <chapter eID="Lev.22"/> <div eID="gen4967" type="x-p"/>

entries.15560c3b3fecc7100fffd8185e2bd433d634bf5b: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.1-Lev.22.16">Lev 22:1-16</reference> <div eID="gen1450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1451" type="x-p"/> Reverence for Things Sanctified. - The law on this matter was, (1) that no priest who had become unclean was to touch or eat them (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.2-Lev.22.9">Lev 22:2-9</reference>), and (2) that no one was to eat them who was not a member of a priestly family (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.10-Lev.22.16">Lev 22:10-16</reference>).
entries.d56ef27e91919b92ccb4ff7da4dad137a8042f3c: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.17-Lev.22.20">Lev 22:17-20</reference> <div eID="gen1459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1460" type="x-p"/> Acceptable Sacrifices. - <reference osisRef="Lev.22.18">Lev 22:18</reference>-20. Every sacrifice offered to the Lord by an Israelite or foreigner, in consequence of a vow or as a freewill-offering (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">Lev 7:16</reference>), was to be faultless and male, “for good pleasure to the offerer” (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.1.3">Lev 1:3</reference>), i.e., to secure for him the good pleasure of God. An animal with a fault would not be acceptable.
entries.632bfe1d5a740b09c600394a6f9942611e082040: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.21-Lev.22.22">Lev 22:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen1460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1461" type="x-p"/> Every peace-offering was also to be faultless, whether brought “to fulfil a special (important) vow” (cf. Num 15:3, Num 15:8 : פּלּא, from פּלא to be great, distinguished, wonderful), or as a freewill gift; that is to say, it was to be free from such faults as blindness, or a broken limb (from lameness therefore: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.21">Deu 15:21</reference>), or cutting (i.e., mutilation, answering to חרוּם <reference osisRef="Lev.21.18">Lev 21:18</reference>), or an abscess (יבּלת, from יבל to flow, probably a flowing suppurating abscess).
entries.6ca38111b8aaff62ee14e3e39f25352481c9a289: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.23">Lev 22:23</reference> <div eID="gen1461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1462" type="x-p"/> As a voluntary peace-offering they might indeed offer an ox or sheep that was רקלוּט שׂרוּע, “stretched out and drawn together,” i.e., with the whole body or certain limbs either too large or too small;<note placement="foot">In explanation of these words <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> very properly remarks, that with the Greeks the sacrificial animal was required to be ἀφελής (<hi type="italic">Pollux</hi> i. 1, 26), upon which <hi type="italic">Hesychius</hi> observes, μήτε πλεονάζων μήτε δέων τι τοῦ σώματος.</note> but such an animal could not be acceptable as a votive offering.
entries.6ba4b246f318c47b8f75dad09226e7703e9b19a0: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.24">Lev 22:24</reference> <div eID="gen1462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1463" type="x-p"/> Castrated animals were not to be sacrificed, nor in fact to be kept in the land at all. מעוּך <hi type="italic">compressus</hi>, θλιβίας, an animal with the stones crushed; כּתוּת <hi type="italic">contusus</hi>, θλασίας, with them beaten to pieces; נתוּק <hi type="italic">avulsus</hi>, σπάδων, with them twisted off; כּרוּי <hi type="italic">excisus</hi>, τομίας or ἐκτομίας, with them cut off. In all these different ways was the operation performed among the ancients (cf<hi type="italic">. Aristot. hist. an.</hi> ix. 37, 3; <hi type="italic">Colum</hi>. vi. 26, vii. 11; <hi type="italic">Pallad</hi>. vi. 7). “And in your land ye shall not make,” sc., וגו מעוּך, i.e., castrated animals, that is to say, “not castrate animals.” This explanation, which is the one given by Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. iv. 8, 40) and all the Rabbins, is required by the expression “in your land,” which does not at all suit the interpretation adopted by <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi> and <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, who understand by עשׂה the preparation of sacrifices, for sacrifices were never prepared outside the land. The castration of animals is a mutilation of God’s creation, and the prohibition of it was based upon the same principle as that of mixing heterogeneous things in Lev 19:19.
entries.0369d5b52cce39b6bcb942fde1499f2d048dcb70: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.25-Lev.22.26">Lev 22:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen1463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1464" type="x-p"/> Again, the Israelites were not to accept any one of all these, i.e., the faulty animals described, as sacrifice from a foreigner. “<hi type="italic">For their corruption is in them,</hi>” i.e., something corrupt, a fault, adheres to them; so that such offerings could not procure good pleasure towards them. - In <reference osisRef="Lev.22.26-Lev.22.30">Lev 22:26-30</reference> three laws are given of a similar character.
entries.29b6b010c63fe623b6e3605eb32f50a6bfac586d: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.27">Lev 22:27</reference> <div eID="gen1464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1465" type="x-p"/> A young ox, sheep, or goat was to be seven days under its mother, and could only be sacrificed from the eighth day onwards, according to the rule laid down in <reference osisRef="Exod.22.29">Exo 22:29</reference> with regard to the first-born. The reason for this was, that the young animal had not attained to a mature and self-sustained life during the first week of its existence.<note placement="foot">For this reason the following rule was also laid down by the Romans: <hi type="italic">Suis faetus sacrificio die quinto purus est, pecoris die octavo, bovis tricesimo </hi>(Plin. <hi type="italic">h. n.</hi> 8, 51).</note> <div eID="gen1465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1466" type="x-p"/> This maturity was not reached till after the lapse of a week, that period of time sanctified by the creation. There is no rule laid down in the law respecting the age up to which an animal was admissible in sacrifice. <hi type="italic">Bullocks</hi>, i.e., steers or young oxen of more than a year old, are frequently mentioned and prescribed for the festal sacrifices (for the young ox of less than a year old is called עגל; <reference osisRef="Lev.9.3">Lev 9:3</reference>), viz., as <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings</hi> in <reference osisRef="Lev.23.18">Lev 23:18</reference>; Num 7:15, Num 7:21, Num 7:27, Num 7:33, Num 7:39.; Num 8:8; Num 15:24; Num 28:11, Num 28:19, Num 28:27; Num 29:2, Num 29:8, and as <hi type="italic">sin-offerings</hi> in <reference osisRef="Lev.4.3">Lev 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.14">Lev 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.16.3">Lev 16:3</reference>; - <hi type="italic">sheep</hi> (lambs) of one year old are also prescribed as <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings</hi> in <reference osisRef="Lev.9.3">Lev 9:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.12.6">Lev 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.12">Lev 23:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38">Exo 29:38</reference>; Num 6:14; Num 7:17, Num 7:21, Num 7:27, Num 7:33, Num 7:39., Num 28:3, Num 28:9, Num 28:19, Num 28:27; Num 29:2, Num 29:8, Num 29:13, Num 29:17., as <hi type="italic">peace-offerings</hi> in Num 7:17, Num 7:23; Num 29:35., and as <hi type="italic">trespass-offerings</hi> in Num 6:12; also a yearling <hi type="italic">ewe</hi> as a sin-offering in <reference osisRef="Lev.14.10">Lev 14:10</reference> and Num 6:14, and a yearling <hi type="italic">goat</hi> in Num 15:27. They generally brought older oxen or bullocks for peace-offerings (Num 7:17; Num 23:29.), and sometimes as burnt-offerings. In Jdg 6:25 an ox of seven years old is said to have been brought as a burnt-offering; and there can be no doubt that the goats and rams presented as sin-offerings and trespass-offerings were more than a year old.
entries.208c0dcedeb29001c97b206fcf7985dc20f07951: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.28-Lev.22.30">Lev 22:28-30</reference> <div eID="gen1466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1467" type="x-p"/> The command not to kill an ox or sheep at the same time as its young is related to the law in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.19">Exo 23:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.22.6-Deut.22.7">Deu 22:6-7</reference>, and was intended to lay it down as a duty on the part of the Israelites to keep sacred the relation which God had established between parent and offspring. - In <reference osisRef="Lev.22.29">Lev 22:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.30">Lev 22:30</reference>, the command to eat the flesh of the animal on the day on which it was offered (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.15">Lev 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.5-Lev.19.6">Lev 19:5-6</reference>) is repeated with special reference to the praise-offering.

entries.4fd4879b96d64621141721a6407333533442f1d7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.22.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.22.1" sID="gen12018" type="section"/> <div sID="gen12019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi><hi type="italic"> And the Lord spake unto Moses.</hi> Moses here treats of the accidents whereby pollution is contracted, although a man may be by nature pure and sound. If any labored under natural defects, Moses prohibited them from exercising the sacerdotal office; now, if any extrinsic pollution may have affected a priest, he commands him to abstain from his duties until he shall have been purified. He had already commanded that any unclean person should be separated from the people lest their contagion should infect others; it may therefore seem superfluous to prescribe to the priests what had been universally enjoined. But since men placed in any position of honor are apt to abuse God’s favor as a pretext for sin, lest the sacerdotal dignity might be used as a covering for the indulgence or excuse of scandals, it was necessary to enact an express law, that the priests should not plead their privilege to eat in their uncleanness of the sacrifices which none but the clean might offer. And that their sacrilege might be the more detestable, he denounces death against any who should intrude their pollutions into the sacrifices; for it was necessary to arouse by the fear of punishment, and as it were to drive by violence to their duty those who would not have been otherwise restrained by any religious feeling from making God’s service contemptible. He then enumerates the particular kinds of pollution of which we have before spoken. Whence it appears, that the priests were brought into discipline by this law, lest they should think themselves more free than the rest of the people, thus might indulge themselves in security; and this is afterwards more clearly expressed where God admonishes them to “keep his ordinance,” <note n="194"> <div sID="gen12020" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lat., “</hi><foreign xml:lang="la">Custodiant custodiam meam</foreign>.” <hi type="italic">Ainsworth, “</hi>Keep my charge."<div eID="gen12020" type="x-p"/> </note> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.22.9">ver. 9</reference>:)<hi type="italic"> i.e., </hi>diligently to observe whatever He commanded; and the greater dignity He had honored them with, that the greater should be their study to persevere in the exercises of piety; for he shews them that so far from their sacerdotal rights conducing to the alleviation of their sin, they were more strongly bound by them to keep the Law.<div eID="gen12019" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.22.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen12018" osisID="Lev.22.1" type="section"/>
entries.961a8242d04f050269653bba1744092cfdf7b1c7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.22.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.22.10" sID="gen12021" type="section"/> <div sID="gen12022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10</hi> <hi type="italic">There shall no stranger.</hi> It was also necessary to add this, that the majesty of sacred things might not be impaired; for if it had been promiscuously permitted to all to eat of the sacred bread and the other oblations, the people would have straightway inferred that they differed not from ordinary food. And unless the avarice of the priests had been thus anticipated, <note n="195"> <div sID="gen12023" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ils eussent ttenu foire et marche des viandes, qui leurs fussent demeurees de residu, ce qui n’eust pas este sans grand opprobre</foreign>:” they would have kept fair and market of the meats which remained over to them, which could not have taken place without much scandal. — <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>.<div eID="gen12023" type="x-p"/> </note> an unworthy trade would have prevailed; for banquets would have been see up for sale, and the priest’s house would have been a kind of provision-market. The prohibition, therefore, that the meats offered in sacrifice should be eaten by strangers, was not made so much with reference to them as to the priests, who would have else driven a profitable trade with the offerings, or, by gratifying their guests, would not have hesitated to bring disrepute on the whole service of God. The Law consequently prohibits that either a sojourner, or a hired servant, should eat of them; and only gives this permission to their slaves, and those who were incorporated into their families. Moreover, He counts the priests’ daughters who had married into another tribe as aliens. The sum has this tendency, that whatsoever depends on the service of God should obtain its due reverence; nor could this be the case, if what was offered in the temple were not distinguished from common food. Inasmuch as they were human beings, they were allowed to subsist in the ordinary manner; yet was this distinction necessary, which might savor of the sanctity of Christ. This was the cleanness of the priests as regarded food.<div eID="gen12022" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.22.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen12021" osisID="Lev.22.10" type="section"/>
entries.48b3a24d2ca7f0b9b57f9d5e0b892f68be67e7b5:
14. And if a man eat of the holy thing unwittingly. A question may here arise, why God would have satisfaction made to the priests, if any one should have eaten of the offerings; for they deserved punishment rather than reward, if they had suffered sacred things to be brought into contempt by their promiscuous use. But the error of those is here dealt with, who had not reserved for the priests their lawful share. A portion, as we shall see, was assigned by God, which they were to set aside before they tasted any part of the victim; those, therefore, who had sinned by inadvertency, are commanded by Him to expiate their fault, to restore so much to the priest, and to add a fifth part. And this was done with the object of which we have spoken, lest, if the things offered to God were exposed to common use, religion should be brought into contempt. What follows afterwards, “and they shall not profane the holy things,” I interpret as addressed to the priests themselves; for this sentence is connected with the previous one, in which the injunctions were directed to the priests alone; and this is further confirmed by the next verse, which declares that the whole people would be accomplices in the sin of the priests if they should have polluted the sacred oblations. For thus I take the words, “that they should not suffer the people to bear the iniquity,” or the punishment of the transgression, if the unclean should have touched things offered to God. For as the priest is the mediator of reconciliation to propitiate God towards men, so his impiety is a common iniquity, which brings guilt upon all. The translation which some give, “that they should not lade themselves,”
As in margin of A. V.
is further from the sense, and altogether wrested. Finally, God again declares that in proportion to the greatness of the honor which He had put upon them, would be the heaviness and inexcusableness of the crime, if they acted unworthily of their calling.
